item.title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
item.description: By Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan (Meituan; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development, by Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, and Hexiang Tan, from Meituan and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The premise is that the field evaluates research agents the wrong way. Agents run long closed-loop cycles of proposing changes, executing experiments, reading verifier feedback, and revising, but benchmarks score them on one final number, which hides where progress was gained, where it leaked away, whether accumulated experience helps or hurts later decisions, and whether the harness rather than the model is doing the work. This report decomposes the loop into rule-based process metrics, runs controlled experience-ablation experiments, varies the agent harness, and then asks an LLM judge with human review whether any solution is actually novel. Seven frontier models, thirty-six tasks, three rollouts each, roughly one hundred thousand U.S. dollars in inference spend. That budget buys credibility; read on for what it bought. The setup first. Tasks come from AutoLab in four families: Model Development with seven tasks, System Optimization with fifteen, Puzzle and Challenge with ten, and CUDA with four. Each task ships a correct but deliberately suboptimal starting artifact, an expert reference solution, a wall-clock budget between two and twelve hours, and an automated verifier scoring zero to one against that scale. Seven models were evaluated: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7-Code, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and LongCat-2.0. The main comparison holds Claude Code version 2.1.152 fixed as a shared harness across all models; native harnesses and OpenCode enter only in a dedicated ablation. item.title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
item.description: By Guibin Zhang, Jiayang Lyu, Ran Sun (National University of Singapore; Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation, by Guibin Zhang of the National University of Singapore, Jiayang Lyu of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, and Ran Sun, with co-authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The paper addresses the central design question in self-evolving agents: when a model teaches itself from experience, what should the teacher be allowed to see? On-policy self-distillation answers this today with designer-specified artifacts. The teacher gets verified reasoning traces, or final answers, or environment feedback, or successful sibling rollouts, or retrieved documents, and each variant works somewhere and fails somewhere else. LOPD's move is structural rather than incremental: stop hand-designing the privilege entirely. Compose retrieved raw trajectories into continuous latent tokens, make that composition learnable end-to-end alongside the student, and let gradient descent decide what experience is worth encoding for supervision. After training you throw away everything except the student. The mechanics, concretely. An experience bank stores successful rollouts offline as task descriptions plus compact action-result traces with verbose observations stripped. At training time a dense retriever fetches entries by cosine similarity over task-trace pairs, defaulting to three. A composer then processes each retrieved item: an encoder with trainable LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone maps the task-experience pair into hidden states, and a QFormer-style cross-attention compressor with learned queries squeezes variable-length states into exactly thirty-two continuous latent tokens per experience, ninety-six tokens total.
